title: World Mental Health Day: UAP supporting employees through mental-health training, workplace policies

Blake Wolfe

UAP Inc. is supporting employee well-being on World Mental Health Day and beyond through an holistic wellness program while reinforcing workplace policies to align with Quebec legislation aimed at improving workers’ psychological safety.

The employer’s global health strategy was launched in 2021 amid the coronavirus pandemic, with mental health a key focus of the initiative from day one, says Geneviève Hébert, the company’s senior director of global compensation. She notes mandatory mental-health training was introduced for UAP’s executives and then expanded to include managers and employees.

Read: 2025 Mental Health Summit: Peel Region’s innovative approach to workplace psychological safety

“It was really important for us to reduce stigma and build a psychologically safe culture, so we made the training mandatory. This was a recommendation from our national global health committee . . . and we said yes right away. This is really the type of initiative that helps build understanding and encourages support-seeking for team members and leaders.”

UAP has also increased coverage for mental-health practitioners and expanded the list of eligible specialists to include family and marriage therapists and social workers. It also removed the cap on the number of mental health-related sessions that plan members can access through the employee assistance program.

“Sometimes, what was stopping people is that they’d start under the EAP for four sessions, then would need to start again with another professional and tell their whole story again.”

To bolster future mental-health initiatives, the employer is currently conducting an internal survey to gauge what supports and resources are most needed by employees, says Hébert.

Read: How employers can support psychological safety amid geopolitical instability

“It’s important for us to listen to what our team members are telling us [and following the survey] we are able to design our action plan for the well-being program for the following year.”

With UAP’s workforce divided among office-based, retail and distribution workers, she notes a range of communication methods are required to reach all plan members. For example, a video that was emailed to in-office workers was converted to a comic strip that was displayed in employee break rooms at UAP’s retail and warehouse locations.

The employer has also aligned its workplace policies with Quebec’s Bill 27. As of October 2025, organizations must now include mental health and psychosocial risks in their prevention obligations.

Hébert says UAP has participated in an independent mental-health risk assessment that outlined the positive impact of the company’s mental-health strategy while noting areas for improvement.

“For example, it was highlighted that sometimes the perception of having a large workload can create stress for employees. We’ve organized information sessions for managers on how to open this discussion with team members — such as what’s the real workload versus perceived workload.”
